title: Quiz: Subroutines - Fundamentals
prompt: Test your foundational understanding of inline vs. closed routines, register conventions, and basic linkage.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of using an open (inline) subroutine?
options: It produces more compact machine code.
It avoids the overhead of calling and returning from a separate subroutine.
It allows an unlimited number of arguments to be passed without using memory.
It automatically saves all caller registers.
questions.explanation: An open subroutine is placed directly into the code where it is used, so the program does not need to branch to a separate routine and then return from it. This can make execution more efficient, but it can also make the program larger if the same routine is used in many places.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between inserting the subroutine directly into the code and jumping to a separate location.

questions.question: A program uses the instruction `bl` to call a subroutine. What instruction would normally be used to return to the calling code?
options: `bl`
`ret`
`stp`
questions.explanation: The `ret` instruction returns from a subroutine by transferring control to the return address stored in the link register (`x30`).
questions.hint: The call needs to remember where execution should continue after the subroutine finishes.

questions.question: Under the AArch64 procedure call convention, where are the first eight argument values normally passed to a procedure?
questions.explanation: The registers `x0` through `x7` are used to pass argument values to a procedure. They are also used to hold result values returned by a procedure.
questions.hint: These registers are used for both passing arguments into a procedure and returning results.

questions.question: A subroutine uses a stack frame to keep track of its local data. Which register is conventionally used as the frame pointer (FP) in AArch64?
questions.explanation: In AArch64, `x29` is conventionally used as the frame pointer (FP). It can be used to provide a stable reference point for accessing data in a subroutine's stack frame.
questions.hint: The frame pointer and link register are commonly saved together when setting up a stack frame.

questions.question: What is a key characteristic of a closed subroutine?
options: Its instructions are inserted directly into the program every time it is used.
Its instructions are stored separately and can be called from multiple locations.
Its instructions are evaluated by a macro processor at runtime.
Its instructions are pushed onto the stack whenever the subroutine is called.
questions.explanation: A closed subroutine is stored as a separate sequence of instructions. When the program needs to use it, control is transferred to that same routine. This avoids duplicating the subroutine's instructions at every point where it is called.
questions.hint: Think about whether the subroutine's instructions are copied into the caller or stored in one separate location.

questions.question: When a `bl` instruction calls a subroutine, what happens to the return address?
options: It is stored in `x29`, the frame pointer.
It is stored in `x30`, the link register.
It is pushed onto the stack automatically.
It is stored in `x0`, the first argument register.
questions.explanation: The `bl` instruction saves the address that execution should return to in `x30`, the link register. When the subroutine finishes, `ret` uses that return address to continue execution in the calling code.
questions.hint: The link register is specifically used to keep track of where the program should return after a subroutine call.
